study.title: Lancet LBP Series 1: what low back pain is, how common, how it runs, and why most cases have no identifiable source
study.evidence_note: A narrative synthesis of mostly systematic-review and cohort evidence. It frames the whole low back pain playbook (non-specific pain, weak imaging-symptom link, red flags that mislead, psychosocial drivers of persistence) rather than testing a treatment.
study.confidence_note: Read the full text in your PDF. The numbers below are as printed in the paper. Some of Table 1 and Table 2 extracted messily from the PDF, so I only quote the cells I could read cleanly. I did not independently re-check the underlying reviews it cites.
study.impact_line: Tell patients: most episodes settle within 6 weeks, but about two-thirds still have some pain at 12 months and a third relapse within a year. A scan finding is a weak guide to the pain source. Screen fear-avoidance and distress early.
study.summary: This is a narrative review from the Lancet Low Back Pain Series working group (an international, multi-profession expert panel), with searches of MEDLINE, Scopus and regional databases and a stated preference for systematic reviews, large cohorts, guidelines and Global Burden of Disease 2015 data. It reports that low back pain is the leading cause of disability worldwide (60.1 million years lived with disability in 2015, up 54% since 1990) and that the specific nociceptive source cannot be identified in nearly all cases. Some MRI findings under age 50 are more common in people with pain (for example disc bulge, extrusion, Modic type 1, spondylolysis), but they are also common without pain and imaging has not been shown to improve outcomes. Most episodes improve substantially within 6 weeks, yet around two-thirds of people still report some pain at 3 and 12 months and about a third relapse within a year. Persistent disabling pain is better explained by a mix of pain intensity, leg pain, fear avoidance, distress, catastrophising, work and social factors and central pain processing than by tissue findings. Serious pathology is rare (0.9% in an Australian primary-care sample) and single red flags are poor discriminators.
study.bottom_line: Treat most back pain as a variable, recurrent, long-running condition rather than a series of unrelated episodes, and don't promise a tissue diagnosis for a disc or any other structure. Use a small number of well-weighted flags for serious pathology rather than a long checklist, and screen early for fear avoidance, distress and leg pain because they carry the best prognostic signal in the paper.

methods.design: Narrative review (Lancet Series paper 1 of 2). No protocol registration, PRISMA flow or formal risk-of-bias assessment reported. Search terms and dates were not given in detail in the text; a workshop in Buxton, UK in June 2016 set the structure.
methods.setting: International author group (Denmark, Australia, South Africa, Switzerland, Finland, USA, Germany, Netherlands, UK). Evidence base mostly from high-income countries, with deliberate searching for low- and middle-income country data.
methods.participants: No participants of its own. Draws on systematic reviews (for example 33 cohorts, 11,166 people for natural history; 14 case-control studies, 3,097 people for MRI findings), population cohorts, guidelines and GBD 2015.
methods.intervention: Not applicable: no treatment tested. Paper 2 of the series covers treatment.
methods.follow_up: Not applicable. Natural-history data come from cohorts followed to 12 months.
methods.primary_outcome: None. The paper describes definition, burden, causes, course, risk factors and contributors to disability.

results.result: Low back pain caused about 60.1 million years lived with disability, up 54% since 1990. Point prevalence of activity-limiting pain was 7.3% (about 540 million people). Fewer than 28% of cases were in the severe or most severe categories but they accounted for 77% of the disability.
results.meaning: MCID not applicable. Most patients have low disability; a minority carry most of the burden, which supports early identification of the high-risk group.

results.result: Median 1-year prevalence about 37%, peaking in mid-life and higher in women. Around 40% of 9-18 year olds report having had low back pain.
results.meaning: Common in your caseload at all ages, including adolescent athletes.

results.result: Most episodes improve substantially within 6 weeks. By 12 months average pain is low (6 points on a 100-point scale, 95% CI 3 to 10).
results.effect: Mean pain 6/100 (95% CI 3 to 10) at 12 months
results.meaning: Average pain at 12 months is far below any commonly used MCID, but the average hides a persistent minority.

results.result: 67% still report some pain at 3 months and 65% at 12 months.
results.effect: 67% (95% CI 50 to 83) at 3 months; 65% (95% CI 54 to 75) at 12 months
results.meaning: Set the expectation that 'some pain' is the usual state at one year; the goal is function and control, not zero pain.

results.result: About 33% recur. The authors say robust estimates are lacking (7 studies, 1,780 people).
results.meaning: Low certainty. Supports a relapse-prevention conversation at discharge.

results.result: Disc degeneration OR 2.2 (prevalence 34% without pain vs 57% with pain). Disc bulge OR 7.5. Disc protrusion OR 2.7. Disc extrusion OR 4.4. Modic type 1 OR 4.0. Spondylolysis OR 5.1. Annular fissure OR 1.8 and high intensity zone OR 2.1 had CIs crossing 1.
results.effect: Degeneration 2.2 (1.2 to 4.2); bulge 7.5 (1.3 to 44.6); protrusion 2.7 (1.5 to 4.6); extrusion 4.4 (2.0 to 9.7); Modic 1 4.0 (1.1 to 14.6); spondylolysis 5.1 (1.7 to 15.5); fissure 1.8 (0.97 to 3.3); HIZ 2.1 (0.7 to 6.0)
results.meaning: Associations only. Several CIs are very wide and heterogeneity was mostly high. Prevalence of degeneration, protrusion and bulge is substantial in people without pain, so a finding cannot tell you the pain source.

results.outcome: Serious pathology in acute primary care
results.result: Specific causes in 0.9% (11 people), 8 of 11 fractures and 2 of 11 inflammatory disorders. About 80% of people with acute back pain have at least one red flag despite under 1% having serious disease.
results.meaning: Single red flags have very low specificity. Use combinations and clinical judgement.

results.outcome: Prognostic factors for chronic disabling pain
results.result: Fear avoidance median LR 2.2 (range 1.5 to 4.9) at 3-6 months and 2.5 (2.2 to 2.8) at 12 months. High pain intensity LR 1.7 at 3-6 months and 1.3 at 12 months. Leg pain LR 1.4 at both. Catastrophising OR 1.56 (1.05 to 2.33) for disability. Number of previous episodes LR 1.0 to 1.1.
results.meaning: Even the best single factor (fear avoidance) shifts probability only modestly. The authors say the table was not systematic.

results.result: Average variance explained in seven development samples was 43%. Pain intensity, psychological distress and leg or multisite pain were the consistent predictors.
results.meaning: More than half of who goes on to disability is unexplained by what we measure, so prognostic tools should inform, not decide.

key_numbers.label: Still in some pain at 12 months (95% CI 54 to 75; 33 cohorts, 11,166 people)
Recurrence within 1 year (Authors note estimates are not robust)
Serious cause in acute primary care (Australian sample of 1,172; 8 of 11 were fractures)
Fear avoidance LR at 12 months (Range 2.2 to 2.8 for chronic disabling pain)

pico.p: People of any age with low back pain, mostly from high-income countries
pico.i: Not applicable (descriptive review of burden, causes, course and risk factors)
pico.o: Prevalence, disability, natural history, imaging associations, prognostic factors

study.limits: A narrative review: selection of studies was not systematic and no risk-of-bias assessment was done on included work. Prognostic table is explicitly not from a systematic review. Most evidence is from high-income countries. Association data (MRI, risk factors, case-crossover) don't show causation, and the authors say causal pathways remain unclear. It was published in March 2018, so it predates later trials and guideline updates.

full_text.why: Read in full from Curt's PDF.

how_to_apply: Reset expectations at the first session: most people improve a lot by about 6 weeks, a majority still have some pain at 3 and 12 months, and about a third relapse within a year. Frame success as function, confidence and flare control, not pain-free.

When a patient asks what is 'causing' the pain, say that for nearly everyone the exact source can't be found, and that imaging findings such as degeneration, bulges and protrusions are common in people with no pain. Don't build a disc diagnosis on a scan. This is context for the Atlas 'discogenic' label: treat it as a working classification, not a confirmed source.

Do not order or request imaging on a routine basis. The paper states there is no evidence imaging improves outcomes and that guidelines consistently recommend against routine use. Consider it when the clinical picture points to a serious cause or a surgical question.

Screen early for the factors with the best signal: leg pain, high initial pain intensity, fear avoidance beliefs, distress or catastrophising, and pain at multiple sites. Use a validated short tool you already trust; the paper does not specify one. Use a positive result to adjust the plan toward graded activity, education and self-efficacy, not to label the patient.

For red flags, weigh the whole picture. Keep a low threshold for further assessment with new perianal sensory change or bladder symptoms, or severe bilateral radicular pain. Consider fracture in older patients, long-term corticosteroid users or after trauma, and consider axial spondyloarthritis in people aged 20 to 40 with inflammatory features (morning stiffness better with exercise) and refer to rheumatology if suspected.

What NOT to change: this paper doesn't test any treatment, so it gives no reason to change your exercise dose, manual therapy use or progression criteria. Use it to shape explanation, expectations, imaging stance and screening.
study.applies_to: Adults and adolescents presenting with non-specific low back pain, with or without leg pain, in primary or private musculoskeletal care. Particularly relevant to the education and classification steps of the lumbar playbook.
study.not_for: Deciding treatment choice or dose. Diagnosing a specific tissue source such as 'discogenic' pain. Ruling serious pathology in or out from a single flag. Patients with confirmed fracture, malignancy, infection, cauda equina features or suspected axial spondyloarthritis, who need specific pathways.

appraisal.tool: JBI (critical appraisal checklist for text and opinion papers; adapted for a narrative review)

domains.domain: Source of opinion has standing in the field
domains.reason: Authors are an international group of back pain researchers and clinicians from nine countries, backed by a steering committee and members from many more institutions.

domains.domain: Opinions centre on the population of interest
domains.reason: Squarely about people with low back pain, including adolescents, workers and older adults, and across income settings.

domains.domain: Stated position is the result of an analytical process
domains.reason: Systematic reviews were preferred and sources (MEDLINE, Scopus, Google Scholar, African Index Medicus) are named, but there is no registered protocol, no search dates or strings in the text and no selection or RoB assessment.
Mostly consistent with the cited reviews, but the prognostic table is explicitly not systematic and several conclusions rest on association data.
Over 100 references, mainly systematic reviews, GBD 2015 and large cohorts, with dissenting qualifiers stated (for example imaging findings are common without pain).

domains.domain: Inconsistency with the literature is justified
domains.reason: No major contradictions identified, but I did not re-read the cited reviews, so I can't judge whether any were selectively reported.
The paper points to an appendix for author declarations which was not in the PDF I read.

grade.reason: Narrative review with no systematic selection or appraisal of the source studies; prognostic summary is acknowledged as non-systematic.
Core findings (non-specific pain, recovery in weeks, recurrence, psychosocial predictors) agree across the reviews it cites. Heterogeneity was high for many MRI pooled estimates.
Descriptive evidence on the same population and outcomes of interest. Some evidence comes from low- and middle-income settings and may not transfer to Australia.
Several key estimates have wide CIs (disc bulge OR 7.5, 95% CI 1.3 to 44.6; Modic 1 OR 4.0, 1.1 to 14.6; recurrence has no CI).
Not assessed in the paper and I can't judge it from the text. Left as not serious only because the findings are descriptive and come from many independent sources; treat as uncertain.

appraisal.clinical_significance: No treatment effect, so no MCID comparison applies. The clinically useful facts are the natural history (average pain about 6/100 at 12 months but 65% still with some pain) and the weak diagnostic value of imaging and red flags. The best single prognostic factor in Table 2 (fear avoidance, LR 2.2 to 2.5) only moves probability a moderate amount, so it should inform the plan, not predict an individual. No NNT can be derived.
appraisal.comparator_fairness: Not applicable: there is no intervention or control arm. The comparison groups inside the cited case-control MRI studies are people without pain, and the authors note that age (under 50) matters for interpretation.
appraisal.alternative_explanations: MRI-symptom and risk-factor links are associations that could reflect confounding, reverse causation (pain causing distress or inactivity) or age. The 12-month recovery figures include regression to the mean and natural history by design. The authors themselves state the causal role of risk factors remains unclear.
appraisal.spin: Little spin. The abstract and conclusion match the body: burden is large and growing, nearly all cases are non-specific, most episodes are short but recurrence and persistence are common. The policy line that health care may contribute to burden in high-income countries is an opinion, not a finding of this review. The call for cost-effective, context-specific strategies is not supported by data presented here.
appraisal.fit_with_evidence: Consistent with the Atlas lumbar playbook (non-specific pain, weak imaging-symptom link, psychosocial prognostic factors). The paper itself cites Brinjikji et al 2015 for MRI findings and Foster et al 2018 (Lancet series paper 2) for treatment, and states guidelines consistently recommend against routine imaging. I did not fetch those sources, so treat this as the paper's own account of the literature. It does not support a confirmed 'discogenic' diagnosis: it says no investigation has accurately identified a disc problem as contributing to an individual's pain and that there is no accepted reference standard.
appraisal.external_validity: Reasonable for an Australian private sports-physio caseload on the topics of natural history, imaging stance and psychosocial screening, with Australian data on red flag prevalence (n=1,172 primary care) and Australian authors contributing. Caveats: the pooled data are mixed-age general populations, not active adults or athletes; the MRI associations are for under-50s; and burden and cost sections lean on low- and middle-income and occupational contexts that matter less to your clinic.
appraisal.would_change_my_mind: A prospective, well-powered cohort in active adults showing a clinically testable subgroup (for example disc-related pain) with a validated diagnostic reference standard would weaken the 'source can't be identified' position. Newer cohorts showing meaningfully better or worse 12-month recovery than 35% pain-free would change the expectation-setting numbers. A trial showing early imaging improves outcomes would overturn the imaging stance.
strengths: Broad, multi-professional author group with explicit attention to low- and middle-income evidence
Prefers systematic reviews and large population data over single studies
Reports effect sizes with CIs and is open about uncertainty (recurrence estimates, causal pathways, non-systematic prognostic table)
Practical, quantified statements on red flags, imaging and natural history that map to clinical decisions
weaknesses: Narrative design with no protocol, search dates or selection and quality assessment
Table 2 prognostic overview is explicitly not based on a systematic review
Many pooled MRI estimates have wide CIs and high heterogeneity
Mostly high-income evidence and general-population samples, not athletes
Published 2018, so later evidence is not included
No treatment evidence in this paper
appraisal.funding_conflicts: Not reported in the main text; the paper refers to an appendix for author declarations which was not in the PDF supplied, so I could not read it.

study.patient_explanation: Most back pain settles over a few weeks, but it often hangs around at a low level or comes back, and that's common. Scan findings like wear or bulges show up in lots of people with no pain, so we focus on getting you moving and confident rather than chasing one cause.
open_questions: Which short screening tool best captures fear avoidance and distress in active adults without over-medicalising them?
How do the natural-history figures differ in athletes and highly active adults?
Would a validated clinical rule ever justify a 'discogenic' label, given there is no accepted reference standard?
What is the relapse rate with and without a structured exercise or education programme after recovery?

sources.citation: Hartvigsen J, Hancock MJ, Kongsted A, Louw Q, Ferreira ML, Genevay S, et al. What low back pain is and why we need to pay attention. Lancet 2018;391:2356-67.
